result.answer:
Verdict: SUPPORTED

CSAT contains 4,331 calls, split into 2,866 training, 362 validation, and 1,103 test calls [S:f5cb37b27fa6#4] (paper-1910.10781.pdf, p.2). The held-out set is 362 + 1,103 = 1,465 calls, so the test share is 1,103/1,465 ≈ 75.3%, which is more than 75% [S:f5cb37b27fa6#4]. Training is 2,866/4,331 ≈ 66.2%, which is less than two thirds (≈66.7%) [S:f5cb37b27fa6#4]. The paper reports the counts rather than explicitly stating the percentage thresholds [S:f5cb37b27fa6#4]. Evidence against: none in the supplied passages; the only caveat is that the percentages are derived from the reported counts [S:f5cb37b27fa6#4].

claims.text: The CSAT split has 2,866 training calls.

The CSAT split has 1,103 test calls.
The held-out CSAT calls total 1,465 (362 validation plus 1,103 test).

claims.note: 2866/4331 = 66.17%, below two thirds (66.67%), consistent with span counts.

citations.title: Hierarchical Transformers for Long Document Classification
citations.text:
CSAT dataset consists of US English telephone speech from call centers. For each call in this dataset,
customers participated in that call gave a rating on his experience with agent. Originally, this dataset
has labels rated on a scale 1-9 with 9 being extremely satisfied and 1 being extremely dissatisfied. Fig.
FIGREF16 shows the histogram of ratings for our dataset. As the distribution is skewed towards
extremes, we choose to do binary classification with ratings above 4.5 as satisfied and below 4.5 as
dissatisfied. Quantization of ratings also helped us to create a balanced dataset. This dataset contains
4331 calls and we split them into 3 sets for our experiments: 2866 calls for training, 362 calls for
validation and, finally, 1103 calls for testing.
